title: Stability of an equilibrium
objectives: Decide an equilibrium’s stability from the trace and determinant.

screens.title: A map of every $2 \times 2$ system
screens.prose: Every matrix $\mathbf{A}$ has a trace $\tau = a + d$ and a determinant $\Delta = ad - bc$. Plot it as the point $(\tau, \Delta)$. Drag the point: the caption names the phase portrait of a matrix with that trace and determinant.

screens.title: Why the map works
screens.prose:
The eigenvalues solve $\lambda^2 - \tau\lambda + \Delta = 0$ (`eigen` l2), so

$$\lambda = \frac{\tau \pm \sqrt{\tau^2 - 4\Delta}}{2}, \qquad \lambda_1\lambda_2 = \Delta, \qquad \lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = \tau.$$

$\Delta < 0$: real roots of opposite sign, a saddle. $\Delta > 0$: same sign as $\tau$, so $\tau < 0$ is stable. $\tau^2 > 4\Delta$ gives a node, $\tau^2 < 4\Delta$ a spiral, and $\tau = 0$ a centre.
screens.question: What is $\tau^2 - 4\Delta$ for the two-factor model?

explain.text: $\tau^2 - 4\Delta = 2.25$ and $\sqrt{2.25} = 1.5$, so $\lambda = (-2.5 \pm 1.5)/2 = -0.5$ and $-2$: lesson 10's eigenvalues, read from two numbers.

screens.title: Continuous against discrete
screens.prose: For $\mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$, stability needs every eigenvalue in the left half-plane: real part below 0. For a chain $\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}_k$, as in `eigen` l4, it needs $|\lambda| < 1$. A matrix has eigenvalues 0.9 and $-0.5$.
screens.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: The chain is stable; the differential equation is not

options.why: 0.9 has a positive real part, so $e^{0.9t}$ grows.

options.text: The differential equation is stable; the chain is not
options.why: Both eigenvalues lie inside the unit circle, so $\mathbf{A}^k \to \mathbf{0}$.
The chain shrinks: $0.9^k \to 0$.

hints.text: Continuous: is each real part below 0?
0.9 passes the discrete test and fails the continuous one.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply each test to 0.9.

explain.text: The same matrix can be a stable chain and an unstable flow. Level 4 returns to this when a numerical step turns an equation into a chain.

screens.title: Negative diagonals, still unstable
screens.prose: Two spreads move as $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix}-1&3\\3&-1\end{pmatrix}$. Each one reverts on its own, since both diagonal entries are negative. A colleague calls the system stable. Drag the start.
screens.question: What is the origin?

options.text: Stable, because both diagonal entries are negative
options.why: You read the diagonal. The coupling 3 is larger than the pull 1: $\Delta = 1 - 9 = -8$.
Symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues, so no spiral.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $\Delta$, not just the diagonal.

byKey.stable: You read stability from the diagonal. $\Delta = 1 - 9 = -8$, so one eigenvalue is positive.

explain.text: The eigenvalues are 2 on $(1, 1)$ and $-4$ on $(1, -1)$. The sum of the spreads runs away even though each reverts alone.

screens.title: On the edges of the map
screens.prose: Points on the boundary lines are fragile. The centre $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-4&0\end{pmatrix}$ sits on the $\Delta$ axis. Change its bottom-right entry from 0 to $-0.01$, a sliver of damping.
screens.question: What does the nudged matrix become?

options.why: $\tau = -0.01 \ne 0$: the orbits no longer close.
$\tau^2 = 0.0001 < 16 = 4\Delta$: inside the parabola, so a spiral.
$\tau < 0$, so it decays.

feedback.correct: $\tau = -0.01$, $\Delta = 4$: just left of the axis, a stable spiral.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the new $\tau$ and $\Delta$.

explain.text: A centre is stable but not asymptotically stable: paths circle and never settle. Any nudge to its trace makes it a spiral, in or out. $\Delta = 0$, a zero eigenvalue, is the other fragile edge.

Order matters: a saddle has any $\tau$, so test $\Delta$ before $\tau$.


screens.title: Check the drift before you simulate
screens.prose: A desk's two-factor model has drift $\mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$ with the matrix shown. Before simulating it as mean-reverting, the quant checks every eigenvalue. Here $\tau = -0.5$ and $\Delta = 0.06 - 0.2 = -0.14$.
screens.question: What is the larger eigenvalue?

byKey.neg: That is the smaller one. The larger is positive.
byKey.tau: You took $\tau/2$ and dropped the square root.

explain.text: $\Delta < 0$ already says saddle, and the eigenvalue 0.2 confirms a direction that grows. The simulation would drift away; the model must be refitted. A vector autoregression is checked the same way, with $|\lambda| < 1$.

ideas: $\tau$ and $\Delta$ fix the eigenvalues through $\lambda^2 - \tau\lambda + \Delta = 0$, so they fix the picture.
$\Delta < 0$ is a saddle; $\Delta > 0$ with $\tau < 0$ is stable, a node below the parabola $\tau^2 = 4\Delta$ and a spiral above it.
Continuous time needs real parts below 0; a discrete chain needs $|\lambda| < 1$.
